title: Owen's Defense | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naro

moves.spoken: This is Owen's Defence — and whatever system you choose, the one constant is that the central pawn must be defended. The simplest way is the knight to c3, doing exactly that while developing.

The subtle choice is to develop the knight to e2 rather than its natural square, in order to connect the knights — so that if one is traded for the other, the pawn structure stays intact. The real concern isn't the trade; it's the central pawn turning into a weakness.
A rook-pawn to a3 forces the opponent to capture, handing over the bishop pair — and two bishops are an asset well worth the little tempo. Put the question and collect the pieces.

Once the opponent castles, don't reflexively lunge the bishop, which would allow a knight to interpose and shove it back. Instead swing the queen to g4 — anticipating a kingside attack, that probing move is remarkably hard to meet. Then apply whole-board awareness: after forcing the enemy queen back, notice a pawn on the far wing left undefended, and pile onto it with a knight that can't be chased off — a classic idea in cramped positions where the defender simply can't marshal a defence in time. A pawn up, take the foot off the gas and make general improving moves — a rook to the open file, preparing a lift, and chasing the intruding knight with a pawn. And keep looking for checks and for the drawback of every enemy pawn push, since advancing a pawn weakens a diagonal a bishop check can exploit. The one caution learned the hard way: don't get so intoxicated by combinations that you start playing unobjectively — the cleanest mate is often the quiet rook infiltration, not the flashiest try.

For the theory record, the bishop pin here is an inaccuracy, because it walks straight into the whole plan — the more flexible route is to develop the knight and strike in the centre, reaching a French-like structure with counterplay to come.

The underrated concept threading the whole game is using the queen — out to g4 or b3 — to poke and prod at weaknesses from a distance. The dream is to provoke a kingside pawn move that weakens the dark squares and opens the door for the bishop to invade. Patience: castle, then set the bait rather than grabbing at it, identify the drawback, and improve.
